before.content_html:
The Framework of Movement

The human skeleton is a living structure made of 206 bones that provides the framework for every movement you make in sport. Without it, muscles would have nothing to pull against. The skeleton works in partnership with the muscular system: muscles contract and pull on bones, which act as levers, creating movement at joints. Understanding which bones are where — and what they do — underpins everything else in PE.

Bones of the Skeleton: Head to Toe

Working from the top of the body downwards, the cranium sits at the very top of the head, curving down around the brain. Below it, the vertebrae form a column of 33 bones running from the base of the skull to the pelvis — protecting the spinal cord and giving the trunk both stability and a controlled range of movement.

At the shoulder, two bones are key. The scapula (shoulder blade) is a flat, triangular bone that sits across the upper back, providing attachment points for the muscles that control the shoulder. The humerus is the long bone of the upper arm, running from the shoulder joint down to the elbow. Together, the scapula and humerus form the shoulder joint — a ball-and-socket joint that allows the greatest range of movement in the body.

At the elbow, three bones meet. The humerus comes down from the shoulder. The radius runs along the thumb side of the forearm, and the ulna runs along the little-finger side. The elbow joint between the humerus and the ulna is a hinge joint allowing flexion and extension. The radius also rotates around the ulna to allow the forearm to turn palm-up or palm-down, a movement essential in racket sports.

Key Fact

Ball-and-socket joints are found at the hip (pelvis and femur) and shoulder (scapula and humerus). Hinge joints are found at the elbow (humerus, radius, ulna), knee (femur and tibia) and ankle (tibia, fibula and talus).

Moving to the lower body, the pelvis is a large basin-shaped structure of fused bones at the base of the spine. It forms the hip joint with the head of the femur — a ball-and-socket joint that allows the greatest range of movement in the lower limb. At the knee, the femur articulates with the tibia (the large shin bone), forming a hinge joint. The patella sits in front of the knee joint, protecting it and improving the mechanical advantage of the quadriceps muscle. The fibula runs alongside the tibia on the outer side of the lower leg, providing a point of attachment for muscles but bearing very little weight. Finally, the talus links the lower leg to the foot, sitting between the tibia and fibula above to form the ankle joint.

The Six Functions of the Skeleton

The skeleton does far more than hold the body upright. It serves six distinct functions, each of which can be applied directly to sport and physical activity.

Support — the skeleton holds the body upright against gravity. A sprinter’s lower limbs support their entire body weight as they drive off the blocks. Without a rigid skeletal frame, the muscular system would have nothing to act on.

Protection — flat bones protect vital organs. The cranium shields the brain; the ribs and sternum form a cage around the heart and lungs. In contact sports such as rugby, the ribcage absorbs impact forces that would otherwise damage the heart and lungs directly.

Movement — bones act as levers. When the biceps contracts during a bicep curl, the forearm bones (radius and ulna) pivot at the elbow to lift the load. In kicking a football, the femur swings at the hip and the tibia swings at the knee, producing explosive leg extension.

The spec distinguishes between long bones and short bones in terms of movement. Long bones such as the femur, tibia, humerus, radius and ulna enable gross movements — the large, powerful movements used in sprinting, jumping and throwing. Short bones, such as those in the wrist and ankle, enable finer, more controlled movements. Flat bones such as the cranium, ribs and scapula serve a protective function and provide broad surfaces for muscle attachment.

The shape and design of each bone directly determines how much movement it allows. The rounded head of the femur fits into the cup-shaped socket of the pelvis, allowing movement in all directions at the hip. The pulley-shaped end of the humerus fits into the groove of the ulna at the elbow, restricting movement to a single plane (flexion and extension only).

Attachment for muscles — the skeleton provides attachment points for muscles. Tendons connect muscles to bones at these points. When a muscle contracts, it pulls on its attachment point and the bone moves. Without firm attachment points, muscular contractions would produce no movement at all.

Mineral storage — bones store calcium and phosphorus. These minerals are released into the bloodstream when the body needs them, and exercise that loads the skeleton — such as weight training or running — stimulates the bones to increase their mineral density, making them stronger over time.

Blood cell production — red bone marrow inside flat and irregular bones produces red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets. Red blood cells carry oxygen to the working muscles during exercise via haemoglobin. This function links directly to cardiovascular performance: a well-functioning skeletal system supports oxygen delivery to muscles.

Key Fact

The six functions of the skeleton are: support, protection, movement, attachment for muscles, mineral storage and blood cell production. Each one can be applied to sport — for example, the femur acts as a lever during kicking (movement) and the ribs protect the lungs during a tackle (protection).

A common mistake is to write only about support and movement when asked for skeletal functions. The mark scheme rewards all six, so always aim for a wider range. Remember that flat bones protect organs (ribs protect the heart and lungs) and that the skeleton is a living structure involved in mineral storage and blood cell production. In a 6-mark analyse question, linking blood cell production to oxygen delivery for aerobic exercise would place you in the top band.

before.content_html:
Why Muscles Work in Pairs

Muscles can only pull — they cannot push. Because of this, every joint in the body is controlled by at least two muscles that work in opposite directions. When one muscle contracts and shortens to produce movement, the opposing muscle relaxes and lengthens to allow that movement. This arrangement is called an antagonistic muscle pair. Understanding these pairs — and always naming them in the context of a specific joint and a specific direction of movement — is essential for exam answers.

Major Muscles of the Body

At the shoulder, the deltoid forms the rounded cap of the shoulder. It is the prime mover for abduction of the arm (lifting it out to the side) and also contributes to flexion and extension. The rotator cuffs are a group of four muscles that wrap around the shoulder joint, stabilising the ball-and-socket joint and assisting rotation — critical in throwing sports such as cricket bowling and javelin. The pectorals (chest muscles) lie across the front of the thorax and act as prime movers in horizontal adduction, such as in the push-up or front crawl pull phase. The latissimus dorsi (‘lats’) is the large fan-shaped muscle of the back, responsible for extension and adduction of the arm at the shoulder, powerful in swimming and rowing movements.

At the elbow, the biceps sits on the front of the upper arm. During elbow flexion (the upward phase of a bicep curl), the biceps is the agonist (prime mover), contracting concentrically to shorten and pull the forearm up. On the back of the upper arm sits the triceps. During elbow flexion, the triceps acts as the antagonist, relaxing and lengthening to allow movement. The roles reverse completely during elbow extension (the downward phase of a press-up): the triceps becomes the agonist and the biceps becomes the antagonist.

At the hip and knee, two large muscle groups dominate. The quadriceps group (four muscles on the front of the thigh) is the prime mover for knee extension — straightening the knee. The hamstrings lie on the back of the thigh and are the prime mover for knee flexion (bending the knee). At the knee, the quadriceps and hamstrings form the classic antagonistic pair: quadriceps agonist during extension, hamstrings agonist during flexion. The gluteals are the large buttock muscles that drive hip extension — critical in sprinting and jumping. The hip flexors are the antagonists to the gluteals, acting as agonists during hip flexion (lifting the knee forwards in running).

At the ankle, the gastrocnemius runs from behind the knee down to the heel via the Achilles tendon. It is the prime mover for plantar flexion — pointing the toes down, as in sprinting push-off or jumping. The tibialis anterior on the front of the lower leg is the prime mover for dorsiflexion (pulling the toes upward), and the two muscles form an antagonistic pair at the ankle.

The abdominals are the core muscles on the front of the trunk. They flex the spine, stabilise the pelvis during running and throwing, and are active in almost every sporting movement as a postural stabiliser.

Key Fact

In a bicep curl upward phase: biceps = agonist (concentric contraction), triceps = antagonist. In kicking (knee extension): quadriceps = agonist, hamstrings = antagonist. In a sprinting push-off (plantar flexion): gastrocnemius = agonist, tibialis anterior = antagonist.

A very common error in exams is to name a single muscle as ‘the agonist’ without specifying the joint, the direction of movement, or the antagonist. Mark schemes award marks for the complete picture: agonist named (1), antagonist named (1), action described at the correct joint (1). Writing ‘the biceps is the agonist’ alone will not earn full marks. Always frame answers as: “During elbow flexion, the biceps acts as the agonist (prime mover) while the triceps acts as the antagonist at the elbow joint.”

Types of Muscle Contraction

Muscles do not always contract in the same way. The spec identifies three types of contraction: isotonic concentric, isotonic eccentric and isometric.

Isotonic concentric contraction occurs when a muscle shortens while it contracts, producing movement. The biceps during the upward phase of a bicep curl contracts concentrically — it shortens, and the elbow flexes. This is the most obvious form of contraction in sport: the quadriceps contracts concentrically to extend the knee when kicking a ball.

Isotonic eccentric contraction occurs when a muscle produces tension while it lengthens. This happens when the muscle is acting as a brake. During the downward phase of a bicep curl, the biceps contracts eccentrically — it is still producing tension to control the lowering of the weight, but it is getting longer as the elbow extends. Eccentric contractions are responsible for DOMS (delayed onset muscle soreness) because the lengthening under load causes tiny tears in muscle fibres.

Isometric contraction occurs when a muscle is active but the joint does not move. A gymnast holding a crucifix position on the rings keeps the arms outstretched perfectly still — the deltoids and pectorals are working hard isometrically. A rugby player locked in a scrum uses isometric contractions to maintain position against an opposing force.

Key Fact

Concentric = muscle shortens (produces movement). Eccentric = muscle lengthens under tension (controls or brakes movement). Isometric = muscle produces tension but no joint movement occurs. All three can happen in the same exercise: a squat involves concentric quadriceps on the way up, eccentric on the way down, and isometric if you pause at the bottom.

Tendons are strong, inelastic connective tissues that attach muscles to bones. Without tendons, a muscle contraction would not move the skeleton. The Achilles tendon, for example, attaches the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles to the calcaneus (heel bone). When the calf muscles contract concentrically, the Achilles tendon transmits the force to the heel, producing plantar flexion for sprinting. Tendons are denser and less elastic than muscles, which is why they take longer to strengthen with training. Overloading tendons without adequate rest is a common cause of injury in growing athletes.

lessons.title: Synovial Joints and Types of Movement

before.content_html:
What Is a Synovial Joint?

Every freely movable joint in the body — at the shoulder, elbow, hip, knee and ankle — is a synovial joint. Synovial joints are the most common type of joint in the body, and they all share the same basic structure: a capsule surrounding the joint, fluid inside to reduce friction, and a range of soft-tissue structures that hold the joint together and prevent injury. Understanding these structures is important not just for anatomy, but for explaining how joints withstand the demands of sport.

Structures of a Synovial Joint

The outer shell of a synovial joint is the joint capsule. It is made of tough, fibrous connective tissue that wraps completely around the joint, forming a sealed envelope. The joint capsule holds the bones in position and contains the joint fluid.

Inside the capsule, the synovial membrane lines the inner surface of the capsule. Its job is to produce synovial fluid — a viscous, egg-white-like substance that coats the ends of the bones inside the joint. This fluid dramatically reduces friction, allowing bones to glide smoothly past each other. Without synovial fluid, the grinding of bone on bone would cause rapid joint damage. During the warm-up phase of exercise, synovial fluid becomes less viscous and spreads more effectively, which is one reason why warming up reduces injury risk.

Covering the ends of the bones inside the joint is articular cartilage, a smooth, bluish-white tissue that absorbs compressive forces and provides an almost frictionless surface. Cartilage has no blood supply of its own — it relies on synovial fluid for nourishment. Once damaged, cartilage heals very slowly, which is why cartilage injuries (such as a torn meniscus in the knee) can end sporting careers.

Ligaments are short, tough bands of fibrous tissue that connect bone to bone across the joint. They are the primary restraints against excessive movement — without them, joints would be unstable. The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) inside the knee, for example, prevents the tibia from sliding forward relative to the femur during landing from a jump. A ruptured ACL is one of the most serious injuries in contact sport.

Tendons do not form part of the synovial joint structure itself, but they pass close to most joints and contribute to stability. The Achilles tendon at the ankle and the patellar tendon at the knee are essential force transmitters from muscle to bone.

Bursae (singular: bursa) are small cushioning sacs filled with fluid. They sit at points where tendons or ligaments would otherwise rub against bone, such as at the front of the knee (the prepatellar bursa). Inflammation of a bursa, known as bursitis, is a common overuse injury in sports that involve repeated kneeling or shoulder work.

Key Fact

The six key structures of a synovial joint are: synovial membrane (produces fluid), synovial fluid (reduces friction), joint capsule (encloses and seals the joint), bursae (cushion tendons against bone), cartilage (absorbs compression and provides frictionless surface), and ligaments (connect bone to bone for stability).

Types of Synovial Joint

The spec identifies two types of synovial joint relevant to GCSE PE. A hinge joint permits movement in one plane only — flexion and extension. The elbow (humerus articulating with the ulna and radius), the knee (femur articulating with the tibia) and the ankle (tibia and fibula articulating with the talus) are all hinge joints. A ball-and-socket joint permits movement in multiple planes. The shoulder (head of the humerus fitting into the glenoid cavity of the scapula) and the hip (head of the femur fitting into the acetabulum of the pelvis) are ball-and-socket joints.

Types of Movement at Synovial Joints

Flexion is a decrease in the angle at a joint — bending. Extension is an increase in the angle — straightening. Both occur at the shoulder, elbow, hip and knee. At the elbow, flexion and extension are the only movements possible because it is a hinge joint. At the shoulder and hip (ball-and-socket), a much wider range of movements is available.

Abduction is movement of a limb away from the midline of the body — lifting the arm out to the side in a star jump. Adduction is movement towards the midline — bringing the arm back down. Both abduction and adduction are available at the shoulder and hip (ball-and-socket joints) but not at the elbow or knee (hinge joints).

Rotation of the shoulder is turning the arm in or out along its long axis. A cricket bowler’s bowling arm rotates at the shoulder during delivery. Circumduction of the shoulder is a circular movement combining flexion, abduction, extension and adduction in sequence — the arm traces a full cone shape. Throwing a javelin involves circumduction of the shoulder.

At the ankle, the movements are named differently. Plantar flexion is pointing the foot downward (pressing the toes away from the body). A sprinter’s powerful push-off at the end of each stride is driven by plantar flexion at the ankle. Dorsiflexion is pulling the toes upward towards the shin — the ankle bends when a gymnast lands from a vault. Both plantar flexion and dorsiflexion are hinge movements at the ankle joint.

Key Fact

Shoulder (ball-and-socket): flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, rotation, circumduction. Knee (hinge): flexion and extension only. Ankle (hinge): plantar flexion and dorsiflexion only. The more movements a joint allows, the greater the sporting versatility — but often at the cost of stability.

A 4-mark exam question might ask how the structures of a synovial joint help prevent injury during sport. A well-developed answer links each structure to its protective role: ligaments prevent bones from moving too far out of alignment (stabilising the knee in a tackle); bursae prevent tendons from rubbing on bone during repeated movements (protecting the knee during cycling); cartilage absorbs impact forces when landing from a jump; synovial fluid lubricates the joint and reduces the wear on cartilage surfaces during sustained aerobic exercise. Always name the structure, state what it does, and give a sporting example.

As body temperature rises during a warm-up, synovial fluid becomes less viscous and distributes more evenly across the joint surfaces. This increases the range of movement available and reduces friction, meaning joints can work more efficiently. Ligaments and tendons also become more pliable at higher temperatures, reducing the risk of tears. This is the physiological reason why a warm-up includes a pulse raiser and stretching before high-intensity work.

lessons.title: Short and Long Term Effects of Exercise

before.content_html:
Three Timescales of Change

Exercise affects the body across three distinct timescales, and your ability to distinguish between them is frequently tested. Immediate effects occur during the exercise session itself. Short-term effects appear in the hours following exercise, typically lasting up to 36 hours. Long-term effects emerge only after months or years of consistent training and represent genuine physiological adaptation. Mixing these up in an exam will cost marks, so developing a clear mental map of which changes belong to which category is essential.

Immediate Effects: What Happens While You Exercise

As soon as exercise begins, several changes are immediately visible or measurable. The skin becomes hot, sweaty and flushed (red): core body temperature rises as the working muscles generate heat, and the body responds by directing blood to the skin capillaries, where heat can radiate away. Sweating further cools the skin through evaporation. The increase in depth and frequency of breathing is driven by rising carbon dioxide levels in the blood: chemoreceptors detect this and signal the respiratory centre to increase breathing rate and tidal volume, delivering more oxygen and removing CO2 more rapidly. Finally, heart rate rises to pump more oxygenated blood to the working muscles — this increase begins even before exercise with an anticipatory rise, driven by adrenaline release, and climbs further as exercise intensity increases.

Key Fact

The three immediate effects of exercise are: (1) hot, sweaty and red skin; (2) increased depth and frequency of breathing; (3) increased heart rate. These all begin during the exercise session and return to normal within minutes of stopping.

Short-Term Effects: The Hours After Exercise

In the period immediately after exercise and for up to 36 hours, the body experiences a range of short-term effects as it recovers. Tiredness and fatigue result from the depletion of glycogen (stored glucose) in the muscles and the accumulation of waste products. Light-headedness can occur as blood redistributes away from the brain toward the muscles during exercise, or when exercise stops suddenly and blood pools in the lower limbs before circulation fully adjusts. Nausea may follow high-intensity efforts, particularly in the stomach, as blood flow to the digestive system is significantly reduced during exercise. Aching, cramp and most importantly DOMS (delayed onset muscle soreness) develop as the micro-damage to muscle fibres — especially after eccentric contractions or unfamiliar movements — triggers an inflammatory response that peaks 24–48 hours post-exercise.

DOMS is caused by micro-tears in the muscle fibres, particularly following eccentric (lengthening) contractions — for example, lowering a weight under control, running downhill or landing from a jump. These micro-tears are repaired by the body, and during that repair process the muscle fibres are rebuilt slightly thicker and stronger than before. This is the fundamental mechanism of muscle hypertrophy. Experienced athletes experience less DOMS because their muscles have already adapted to a given level of stress. When DOMS does appear, it is typically a signal that a new training stimulus has been applied and adaptation is underway — but the soreness itself should not be severe enough to limit movement significantly.

Long-Term Effects: Adaptations From Months of Training

Consistent exercise over months and years causes permanent physiological adaptations in multiple body systems. These long-term effects represent the body becoming structurally and functionally more efficient at the demands placed on it.

Body shape may change: regular resistance training increases muscle size and reduces relative body fat, while prolonged endurance training may produce a leaner physique with visible muscular definition. Specific components of fitness improve: muscular endurance, speed, suppleness, muscular strength, cardiovascular endurance and stamina all increase with appropriately designed training programmes. For example, a sprinter who trains over many months will improve their speed and explosive strength; a cross-country runner will develop greater cardiovascular endurance and muscular endurance in their legs.

Two of the most significant long-term cardiovascular adaptations are cardiac hypertrophy and bradycardia. Cardiac hypertrophy refers to the heart growing larger and stronger as a muscle in response to the repeated demands of training. A larger, stronger heart can pump more blood per beat — a greater stroke volume. Because stroke volume is higher, the heart does not need to beat as many times per minute to deliver the same cardiac output. This produces bradycardia: a lowered resting heart rate. While the average untrained person has a resting heart rate of around 60–80 beats per minute, elite endurance athletes such as cyclists or distance runners may have resting heart rates of 35–50 bpm. Mo Farah, for example, is reported to have had a resting heart rate in the low 40s during the peak of his marathon career.

Key Fact

The chain: regular training → cardiac hypertrophy (the heart grows larger) → greater stroke volume per beat → bradycardia (lower resting heart rate needed to maintain cardiac output). These are all long-term adaptations — they take months or years of consistent training to develop.

Hypertrophy as a general term refers to the growth in size of a muscle caused by an increase in the size of individual muscle fibres. When applied to skeletal muscles (e.g. the biceps or quadriceps group), it is the result of progressive resistance training: repeated eccentric and concentric contractions under load cause micro-tears, which repair larger and stronger over time. When the term is used specifically as “cardiac hypertrophy,” it refers to the same growth process applied to the heart muscle itself, driven by the sustained cardiovascular demands of endurance training. In both cases, the underlying stimulus is the same — the body adapts to repeated stress by growing the muscle tissue — but the practical outcomes differ: skeletal muscle hypertrophy increases strength and power for movement, while cardiac hypertrophy increases stroke volume and reduces resting heart rate.

What Is a Lever System?

The human body is a machine built from levers. Every time you kick a ball, perform a push-up or rise onto your toes, you are using a lever system to transmit force. Understanding how levers work allows coaches and athletes to explain why some movements generate great force, and why others allow great speed but require more effort. A lever consists of three components arranged around a pivot point. The fulcrum is the fixed pivot point — in the body, a joint. The load (also called the resistance) is the weight or force being moved. The effort is the force applied to move that load — in the body, this is the force produced by the contracting muscle. The three classes of lever differ in the relative positions of these three components: fulcrum (F), load (L) and effort (E).

Key Fact

The three lever classes by component order along the lever bar: First class — Fulcrum between Load and Effort (FLE / EFL). Second class — Load between Fulcrum and Effort (FLE with load in the middle). Third class — Effort between Fulcrum and Load (FEL). A reliable mnemonic: first class has F in the middle; second class has L in the middle; third class has E in the middle.

First Class Levers

In a first class lever, the fulcrum sits between the load and the effort. Think of a seesaw: the pivot is in the middle, with weight on one side and the pushing force on the other. In the body, the clearest example is the nodding action of the head at the atlantooccipital joint: the skull (load) rests at one end of the vertebral column, the neck muscles (effort) pull from behind, and the joint itself (fulcrum) sits between them. Another example is elbow extension during a push-up: the triceps apply effort at the olecranon behind the elbow joint (fulcrum), moving the weight of the forearm and body (load) on the other side. First class levers can produce both force and speed depending on where the effort and load arms fall.

Second Class Levers

In a second class lever, the load sits between the fulcrum and the effort. The classic everyday example is a wheelbarrow: the wheel is the fulcrum at one end, the load sits in the middle, and your hands apply effort at the handles. In the body, plantar flexion at the ankle — rising onto the toes — is the textbook second class lever: the ball of the foot acts as the fulcrum, the body weight (load) acts through the ankle joint in the middle, and the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles (effort) pull via the Achilles tendon at the heel, which is behind and above the load. Second class levers always produce a mechanical advantage greater than 1, meaning the effort arm is longer than the load arm, so a relatively small muscular effort can move a larger load. This makes them excellent for force production but not for speed.

Third Class Levers

In a third class lever, the effort is applied between the fulcrum and the load. This is the most common lever arrangement in the human body. The classic example is elbow flexion during a bicep curl: the elbow joint is the fulcrum, the biceps apply effort just below the elbow joint, and the load (the forearm, hand and any weight held) is at the far end. The effort arm (joint to biceps insertion) is shorter than the load arm (joint to hand), which means more muscular effort is needed to move the load. However, a small movement of the biceps produces a large movement of the hand — trading mechanical disadvantage for speed and range of movement. Third class levers therefore favour speed and range over force, which is why most striking and throwing actions in sport use them.

A very common exam error is mis-labelling the positions of the fulcrum, load and effort on a lever drawing, or confusing which class a sporting example belongs to. The mark scheme specifically requires the correct LFE arrangement to be visible on any diagram question. A reliable approach is to identify the joint first (that is always the fulcrum), then identify what is being moved (the load, usually the body part or weight), and finally identify where the muscle pulls (the effort). Once you have these three pinned, the class follows logically: if the joint (F) is between the other two, it is first class; if the weight (L) is in the middle, it is second class; if the muscle pull (E) is in the middle, it is third class. Double-check by asking: “Where is the pivot?” — then label outward from there.

Mechanical Advantage

Mechanical advantage (MA) is a number that tells you whether a lever amplifies force (MA > 1) or amplifies speed and range of movement (MA < 1). The formula is: Mechanical advantage = effort arm ÷ load (resistance) arm. The effort arm is the distance from the fulcrum to the point where effort is applied. The load arm (resistance arm) is the distance from the fulcrum to the point where the load acts.

A mechanical advantage greater than 1 means the effort arm is longer than the load arm — a small effort produces a large force at the load point. This is the case in second class levers, and is why rising onto your toes lifts your entire body weight with relatively modest calf muscle effort. A mechanical advantage less than 1 means the load arm is longer than the effort arm — more muscular effort is required, but the trade-off is greater speed and range. Third class levers have MA < 1. First class levers can have MA either above or below 1, depending on the position of the fulcrum relative to the load and effort arms.

Imagine a simplified model of the elbow during plantar flexion (second class lever). The effort arm (heel to Achilles insertion) measures 6 cm. The load arm (heel to ankle joint) measures 4 cm. Mechanical advantage = effort arm ÷ load arm = 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5. Because MA is greater than 1, the calf muscles need to produce less force than the body weight they are lifting — the lever system amplifies force. Now consider elbow flexion (third class lever). Effort arm (elbow joint to biceps insertion) = 4 cm. Load arm (elbow joint to hand holding a dumbbell) = 30 cm. MA = 4 ÷ 30 = 0.13. The biceps must produce around 7.5 times the load to lift the weight — a significant mechanical disadvantage — but the hand moves through a much greater arc than the biceps shortens, generating the high speed needed for throwing and striking actions.

Key Fact

Mechanical advantage = effort arm ÷ load arm. MA > 1 means force is amplified (second class lever). MA < 1 means speed and range are amplified (most third class levers). In the exam, always show the formula, the substitution, and the units (dimensionless, but arm lengths in cm).

lessons.title: Health, Fitness and the Components of Fitness

before.content_html:
Health and Fitness: Not the Same Thing

Most people use the words “healthy” and “fit” interchangeably, but in sports science they have precise, separate definitions. Health is defined as a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being — not simply the absence of illness. This definition, taken from the World Health Organization, emphasises that a person can feel ill or stressed and still have no diagnosable disease, meaning their health is compromised even if a doctor would not prescribe anything.

Fitness, in contrast, is defined as the ability to meet the demands of the environment. This means that fitness is specific to purpose: a sprinter needs explosive power and speed; a marathon runner needs cardiovascular endurance and muscular endurance; a goalkeeper needs agility, reaction time and explosive strength. A person who is highly fit for one sport may be relatively unfit for another.

Crucially, health and fitness do not always go together. Someone with a serious injury (poor health) can still maintain cardiovascular fitness through swimming. Equally, an elite athlete may be very fit but show signs of overtraining — sleep disruption, hormonal imbalance, low mood — which are all health issues. Understanding this relationship is essential when evaluating the role exercise plays in an individual’s life.

Key Fact

Health = a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being (not merely the absence of disease). Fitness = the ability to meet the demands of the environment. These are two distinct definitions — learn both precisely.

Decreased fitness because of ill health: a footballer recovering from a knee injury cannot train at full intensity, so their cardiovascular fitness and muscular strength decline even though they are otherwise healthy. Increased fitness despite ill health: a competitive cyclist with a managed long-term condition such as asthma can still train rigorously and maintain high cardiovascular endurance, even though their health is not “complete.” These two scenarios show that fitness and health influence each other but are not the same variable — an important distinction in exam questions.

The Ten Components of Fitness

The specification identifies ten components of fitness. No single sport requires all ten in equal measure, so a key skill is identifying which components are most relevant to a given activity and justifying why. The ten components are:

Agility — the ability to change body position quickly and accurately while moving. Essential in team sports such as rugby, basketball and hockey, where players must dodge opponents and change direction at speed.

Balance — the ability to retain the body’s centre of mass over its base of support. Can be static (holding a handstand) or dynamic (a gymnast on a balance beam). Important in gymnastics, surfing, skiing and judo.

Cardiovascular endurance (also called aerobic power) — the ability of the heart and lungs to supply oxygen to working muscles during sustained exercise. This is the foundation of performance in long-distance running, rowing, cycling, football and many other activities.

Coordination — the ability to use two or more body parts together smoothly and efficiently. Vital in cricket (eye-hand coordination for batting), tennis (eye-hand for racket sports) and swimming (synchronising arms and legs).

Flexibility — the range of movement possible at a joint. Crucial in gymnastics, dance, swimming (stroke efficiency) and martial arts. Poor flexibility can limit performance and increase injury risk.

Muscular endurance — the ability of a muscle to undergo repeated contractions over a long period without tiring. Important in rowing, cycling and long-distance swimming, where the same muscle groups perform thousands of repeated actions.

Power (also called explosive strength or anaerobic power) — the ability to exert maximum force in as short a time as possible; it combines strength and speed. Power is critical in sprinting, shot-put, jumping events and boxing.

Reaction time — the time taken to initiate a response to a stimulus. A sprinter reacting to the starting gun, a goalkeeper responding to a shot, and a batsman reading a delivery all depend on a fast reaction time.

Strength — the maximum force a muscle or muscle group can exert in a single effort. The specification identifies four types: maximal strength (the greatest force in a single effort), static strength (force exerted against an immovable object), dynamic strength (force produced through a full range of movement repeatedly) and explosive strength (maximum force in the shortest time, which overlaps with power).

Speed — the maximum rate at which an individual is able to perform a movement or cover a distance in a period of time. Speed is relevant not just in sprinting but in any sport where rapid movement is an advantage — a winger in football breaking past a defender, for example.

Key Fact

The ten components: agility, balance, cardiovascular endurance, coordination, flexibility, muscular endurance, power, reaction time, strength, speed. Questions often ask you to select components and justify their importance for a specific sport — always name the component AND give a sporting reason.

A 100m sprinter needs: (1) reaction time — to leave the blocks the instant the starter’s pistol fires, reducing overall race time; (2) power — to accelerate explosively from the blocks during the drive phase; (3) speed — to maintain maximum velocity during the top-speed phase; and (4) muscular endurance — to sustain near-maximal effort for the full 10–12 seconds before significant lactic acid accumulation. Cardiovascular endurance is less important than in a marathon because the race duration is too short for the aerobic system to be the limiting factor. In the exam, always justify why the component matters for that specific sport — not just list its name.

Why We Test Fitness

Fitness testing gives coaches and athletes a window into an individual’s current physical condition. Without measurement, training decisions rely on guesswork. With structured testing, a coach can identify which components of fitness are strengths and which need attention, set a baseline from which improvement is tracked, compare results against national norms, and motivate athletes by giving them concrete targets.

The specification identifies six reasons for conducting fitness tests: to identify strengths and weaknesses in performance or a training programme; to monitor improvement over time; to show a starting level of fitness; to inform training requirements; to compare against norms of a group or national averages; and to motivate athletes and help them set realistic goals. A seventh reason is to provide variety in a training programme, as testing sessions can break up routine and maintain engagement.

Key Fact

Seven reasons for fitness testing: (1) identify strengths/weaknesses, (2) monitor improvement, (3) establish a baseline, (4) inform training needs, (5) compare to norms, (6) motivate/set goals, (7) provide variety. In a question, give the reason and a brief example to show you understand it.

The Standard Tests and Their Procedures

For each component of fitness there is a named standard test. You must know the component it measures, the equipment needed and the basic procedure.

Illinois Agility Test — measures agility. The performer lies face down at the start. On a signal they sprint to a set of cones arranged in a specific pattern, weaving in and out, before sprinting back. Time is recorded in seconds. A shorter time means better agility.

Stork Stand Test — measures balance. The performer stands on their dominant leg, places the non-dominant foot against the inside of the dominant knee and raises the heel. They hold this position for as long as possible with eyes open. Time in seconds is recorded.

Multi-Stage Fitness Test (bleep test) — measures cardiovascular endurance. The performer runs back and forth between two lines 20 metres apart in time with an audio signal (bleep). The signal speeds up progressively. The level reached when the performer fails to reach the line twice in a row is their score.

Wall Toss Test — measures coordination. The performer stands at a set distance from a wall and throws a ball with one hand at the wall, catching it with the opposite hand. The number of successful catches in 30 seconds is the score.

Sit and Reach Test — measures flexibility. The performer sits on the floor with legs straight, feet flat against a box with a measuring scale. They reach forward as far as possible and hold the position; the distance reached (in cm) is recorded. A greater distance indicates greater flexibility.

Vertical Jump Test — measures power (explosive strength). The performer stands next to a wall, reaches as high as possible to mark a standing-reach height, then jumps and marks the highest point reached. The difference between the two marks (in cm) is the score.

Ruler Drop Test — measures reaction time. A ruler is held by a partner at 0 cm and the performer places their dominant hand around the ruler without touching it. When the ruler is released without warning, the performer catches it as quickly as possible. The distance the ruler falls before it is caught indicates reaction time — a shorter drop = faster reaction time.

30 Metre Sprint Test — measures speed. The performer sprints 30 metres from a standing start. Time in seconds is recorded using a stopwatch or timing gate. Shorter time = greater speed.

Handgrip Dynamometer Test — measures strength. The performer squeezes a handgrip dynamometer as hard as possible (dominant hand), holding for 5 seconds. The force recorded in kilograms (kg) is the score. Three trials are typically taken and the highest is used.

The Sit-Up Bleep Test measures muscular endurance, and the One Rep Max Test measures maximal strength: the performer performs one maximal lift of a specific exercise (e.g. bench press or squat) — the heaviest weight lifted with correct technique is the score.

Key Fact

Test names by component: agility → Illinois Agility Test; balance → Stork Stand; cardiovascular endurance → Multi-Stage Fitness Test; coordination → Wall Toss; flexibility → Sit and Reach; power → Vertical Jump; reaction time → Ruler Drop; speed → 30 Metre Sprint; strength → Handgrip Dynamometer or One Rep Max.

Quantitative and Qualitative Data

Fitness test results are mostly quantitative data — numbers such as time in seconds, distance in centimetres, or force in kilograms. This numerical data can be compared against national norm tables to see whether a performer is “excellent”, “above average”, “average”, “below average” or “poor” for their age and sex. Qualitative data deals with descriptions rather than numbers — for example, a coach observing that a player “looks sluggish in the second half” is collecting qualitative data.

Fitness tests are a useful guide but have significant limitations. First, most are not sport-specific: the Illinois Agility Test measures agility in a straight-line cone pattern — it does not replicate the unpredictable direction changes of a football match. Second, tests do not replicate competitive conditions: a laboratory Multi-Stage Fitness Test does not replicate the decision-making, adrenaline and contact of a real game. Third, many tests are sub-maximal, meaning the performer is not pushed to their true maximum, so results may under-represent actual capacity. Fourth, motivation affects results: a performer who is uninterested may not try fully on a Ruler Drop or Stork Stand. Fifth, some tests require careful protocol to be valid — the Sit and Reach result is meaningless if the performer has not warmed up their hamstrings first. These limitations must be acknowledged when drawing conclusions from test data.

Validity refers to whether a test actually measures the component it claims to measure. The Ruler Drop Test is valid for reaction time because catching a falling ruler directly requires a fast neural response. However, it may have lower validity for sports that require reactive movements of the whole body (e.g. a goalkeeper’s dive). Reliability refers to consistency: if the same test is repeated under the same conditions, does it produce the same result? To improve reliability, standardise the conditions — same time of day, same warm-up, same equipment, same instructions — and take multiple trials.

practice_questions.text: Identify the fitness test used to measure cardiovascular endurance.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: the Multi-Stage Fitness Test (accept: bleep test or 20-metre shuttle run test).

practice_questions.text: State two limitations of using fitness tests to assess a performer's ability in their sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two distinct limitations from: tests are not sport-specific / do not replicate movements of the activity / do not replicate competitive conditions / many are sub-maximal (therefore may be inaccurate) / motivation of participant affects results / incorrect procedures reduce validity. Two near-identical answers (e.g. 'not sport-specific' and 'doesn't replicate the sport') score only 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Describe how the Ruler Drop Test is conducted and what the score indicates about a performer's fitness.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for describing the set-up (partner holds ruler at the 0 cm end; performer places dominant hand around but not touching the ruler); 1 mark for describing the procedure (ruler is dropped without warning; performer catches it as quickly as possible); 1 mark for explaining the scoring (the distance in cm the ruler falls before being caught indicates reaction time — a shorter distance indicates a faster reaction time).

practice_questions.text: Table 1 shows fitness test results for two 16-year-old county-level athletes before and after a 10-week training block. Athlete A: Illinois Agility Test — before 15.8 s, after 14.2 s. Athlete B: Illinois Agility Test — before 16.1 s, after 15.9 s. Using the data, interpret what the results suggest about the effectiveness of training for each athlete.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for comparing Athlete A's before and after scores (improved by 1.6 seconds); 1 mark for making an inference about Athlete A (training was effective / meaningful improvement in agility); 1 mark for comparing Athlete B's before and after scores (improved by only 0.2 seconds, a marginal change); 1 mark for making a contrasting inference about Athlete B (training had little effect on agility / improvement is negligible and may be within measurement error). Note: accept any valid reference to the figures quoted from the table.

practice_questions.text: A school physical education teacher wants to set up a fitness testing programme for her Year 10 GCSE class. She plans to use the Multi-Stage Fitness Test, the Illinois Agility Test and the Sit and Reach Test. Analyse the benefits and limitations of using this selection of tests to assess the overall fitness of her students.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): identifies and explains genuine benefits for at least two of the three tests (e.g. Multi-Stage Fitness Test provides quantitative cardiovascular endurance data that can be compared to national norms, motivating students with a clear score; Illinois Agility Test is practical in a school setting with minimal equipment; Sit and Reach requires only a box and gives a quick flexibility benchmark); identifies specific limitations for at least two tests (e.g. Illinois test does not replicate sport-specific agility patterns in team games; Sit and Reach reliability is affected by hamstring warm-up and whether students fully extend; Multi-Stage Fitness Test requires motivation to reach maximum level); considers the overall coverage (three tests only cover cardiovascular endurance, agility and flexibility — components like strength, power and reaction time are not assessed); sustained analytical discussion with specific reference to the tests and their sporting relevance.

Secure (3-4 marks): identifies benefits and limitations for most tests; some analysis of what the selection does or doesn't cover; generally accurate.

Developing (2 marks): identifies one benefit and one limitation; limited analysis of coverage.

Emerging (1 mark): one relevant point about a test with minimal development.

practice_questions.text: A sports coach argues that fitness testing should form a central part of every athlete's training programme throughout the year, not just at the start of a season. Evaluate this claim, considering the benefits of regular fitness testing and the potential drawbacks of using it too frequently or in inappropriate contexts.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8-9 marks): evaluates benefits of regular testing (monitors improvement over time and allows training adjustments; motivates athletes by showing progress; identifies when fitness is declining so reversibility can be addressed; provides data to compare against national norms and set goals); evaluates drawbacks of frequent testing (time taken away from actual training; testing fatigue if done too often; results can be demotivating if improvement plateaus; many tests are not sport-specific so results do not directly translate to competitive performance); evaluates context and timing (testing most appropriate at start and end of training blocks; during competition season, maintaining performance is the priority and repeated testing may disrupt preparation); provides a balanced conclusion (regular testing has value when spaced appropriately and limitations are understood; blind reliance on test scores without contextualising them is a mistake); consistent sporting examples throughout.

Secure (6-7 marks): identifies benefits and drawbacks with sporting examples; some consideration of context or timing; generally balanced.

Developing (3-5 marks): some benefits and at least one drawback; limited sporting application.

Emerging (1-2 marks): one relevant point about fitness testing with minimal evaluation.

lessons.title: Principles of Training: SPORT and FITT

before.exam_tip_html: On a “9-mark Evaluate” question about training principles or a training programme, the most common error is writing a one-sided answer: listing only benefits or only limitations. Mark schemes reward a balanced argument with sporting examples on both sides. Structure your answer: state the principle and its benefit for performance, then consider a limitation or a sport where the principle is harder to apply, and link each point to a named sport or athlete scenario. For shorter “define” or “describe” questions, precision matters: “progressive overload” must include the idea that the training load is gradually increased over time, not just that you train harder — one-word answers lose the second mark. Also check: the spec uses “Tedium” as the fourth SPORT principle, not “Thresholds” — this is a common confusion.

On a 9-mark ‘Evaluate’ question about training methods, the most common error is producing a one-sided answer — for example, only listing advantages of a method without weighing its disadvantages or comparing it to an alternative. Examiners reward a balanced argument: present the benefits with a sporting example, then consider the limitations or when another method might be more appropriate. Use a “For X… However Y…” structure throughout and anchor every point to a named sport or named athlete type. For 2-mark ‘State Two’ questions, make sure your two answers are genuinely different — saying “it improves aerobic fitness” and “it improves cardiovascular endurance” is the same point and will only earn one mark.
before.content_html:
Why Choose the Right Training Method?

Not all training is created equal. A marathon runner who only does heavy weight training will not improve her aerobic endurance; a sprinter who only plods along at a slow jog will never develop the explosive power he needs off the blocks. Training must be specific to the demands of the sport — this is the principle of specificity in action. Choosing the correct training method is therefore the first and most important decision a coach or athlete makes when designing a programme.

Continuous Training

Continuous training involves exercising at a steady pace for a minimum of 20 minutes without any rest breaks. Activities such as running, cycling, swimming and rowing are all commonly used. Because the intensity remains constant and the body has a continuous oxygen supply, continuous training primarily develops cardiovascular endurance. It is well suited to distance runners, rowers and cyclists.

The main advantage is that it is simple, low-cost and easy to monitor — a runner simply keeps going at a steady pace within their aerobic training zone (60–80% of maximum heart rate). A disadvantage is that it can become repetitive and may not replicate the varied demands of team sports, which involve bursts of speed interspersed with periods of lower intensity.

Fartlek Training

Fartlek training takes its name from the Swedish for “speed play”. Unlike standard continuous training, fartlek deliberately mixes periods of higher intensity effort with periods of slower recovery running, all without stopping. A footballer might jog steadily for two minutes, then sprint for 30 seconds, then stride at half-pace for a minute, then repeat. Because the performer decides when to change pace, it replicates the unpredictable demands of many team sports.

Key Fact

Fartlek means “speed play” in Swedish. It varies speed and terrain continuously, making it ideal for team-sport athletes whose games combine aerobic and anaerobic demands — such as footballers, rugby players and hockey players.

Interval Training and HIIT

Interval training uses a planned work:rest ratio — a set period of hard effort followed by a set period of rest or low-intensity recovery. The athlete repeats this pattern for a fixed number of sets. For example, a 400 m track athlete might run 200 m at race pace, rest for 90 seconds, and repeat six times. By controlling the work:rest ratio, the coach can target either aerobic or anaerobic systems: longer work periods with short rests challenge the aerobic system, while very short, maximal sprints with longer rests target the anaerobic system.

High-intensity interval training (HIIT) is a specific form of interval training where the work periods are performed at near-maximal intensity (typically above 80% of maximum heart rate, within the anaerobic training zone) and rest periods are short. A typical HIIT session might involve 20 seconds of all-out effort followed by 10 seconds of rest, repeated eight times (the Tabata protocol). HIIT is time-efficient and produces improvements in both aerobic capacity and anaerobic power, making it popular with athletes who are pressed for time.

Many students assume interval training is always anaerobic because of the repeated high-intensity efforts. In fact, the energy system targeted depends entirely on the work:rest ratio and intensity. A 3-minute effort at 65% maximum heart rate, with 1 minute of walking recovery, repeated five times, is aerobic interval training. Anaerobic interval training requires efforts above 80% of maximum heart rate with longer recovery periods. Always identify the intensity and duration to justify which energy system is being stressed — this is exactly the justification examiners look for.

Circuit Training

Circuit training involves moving around a series of stations, performing a specific exercise at each one before moving on to the next. A coach designing a circuit must consider: the space and equipment available, the number of stations, the work:rest ratio at each station, and the type of exercise at each station. The beauty of circuit training is its flexibility — by changing the exercises, the number of stations, the time at each station and the rest periods, the same circuit format can be adapted to develop cardiovascular endurance, muscular endurance, strength or power.

For example, a muscular endurance circuit might include press-ups, sit-ups, squat jumps, tricep dips and step-ups, each performed for 45 seconds with 15 seconds to move to the next station. To make the same circuit develop strength instead, the coach would add resistance (using dumbbells or weighted vests), reduce the repetitions per station and increase the rest periods.

Weight Training

Weight training uses free weights, machines or bodyweight exercises with added resistance to develop muscular strength, power or muscular endurance. The fitness aim determines the weight and repetitions used. For strength and power, athletes use a high weight (above 70% of one rep max) and a low number of repetitions — approximately three sets of four to eight repetitions. For muscular endurance, athletes use a lower weight (below 70% of one rep max) with a high number of repetitions — approximately three sets of 12 to 15 repetitions.

Safe practice is non-negotiable: correct lifting technique prevents injury, appropriate weight selection avoids overloading, and a spotter should be present when performing heavy lifts such as the bench press or squat. The back should remain straight during deadlifts and squats to protect the lumbar vertebrae.

Key Fact

Strength/power training: above 70% of one rep max, approximately 3 sets of 4–8 reps. Muscular endurance training: below 70% of one rep max, approximately 3 sets of 12–15 reps. The fitness aim determines the weight and rep range.

Plyometric Training

Plyometric training develops explosive power. The physiological basis is the stretch-shortening cycle: the muscle first undergoes a rapid eccentric (lengthening) contraction as the athlete lands or prepares, storing elastic energy in the muscle and tendon; this is immediately followed by a powerful concentric (shortening) contraction as the athlete jumps, bounds or throws. The faster the transition between these two phases, the greater the power output. Exercises include bounding, depth jumping, box jumps and medicine-ball throws. Plyometrics is well suited to sprinters, high jumpers, basketball players and volleyball players — any athlete who needs explosive leg or upper-body power.

Static Stretching

Static stretching involves slowly lengthening a muscle to the point of mild discomfort and holding the position for up to 30 seconds. Because the muscle is held in an isometric contraction (no movement, no change in length), this method is categorised as isometric in nature. Static stretching improves flexibility by gradually lengthening the muscle fibres and their surrounding connective tissue over time. It is advisable to avoid bouncing during stretches (ballistic stretching), as this activates the stretch reflex and risks muscle strains. Static stretching is most effective as part of a cool-down rather than immediately before explosive exercise.

Consider a county-level basketball player with a 10-week pre-season. Her coach wants to improve cardiovascular endurance, muscular power and flexibility. An appropriate programme might combine: (1) fartlek training twice a week to mirror the stop-start aerobic and anaerobic demands of a basketball game; (2) plyometric training twice a week (depth jumps and bounding) to improve explosive jumping power for rebounds and lay-ups; (3) static stretching at the end of each session to improve hip and hamstring flexibility, reducing injury risk. Continuous training alone would be insufficient because it would not develop the anaerobic power the sport demands.
